No — that syntax will silently give you the wrong model, and it's one of the most common gotchas in nested MLM work.

The problem is ID non-uniqueness. When student IDs run 1–30 within each classroom, Student 1 in Classroom A and Student 1 in Classroom B are different children, but they share the same value of student_id. When you write (1 | classroom) + (1 | student_id), lme4 treats all rows with student_id == 1 as belonging to the same random-effect level — effectively pooling students across classrooms who share a number. Instead of estimating a random intercept per actual student, it estimates one per numerical label, conflating students from different classrooms into spurious 'super-students'. The model looks like it ran fine and produces no warning, but the student-level variance component is estimated from the wrong grouping.

You have two clean fixes:

Option 1 — Use the explicit nesting syntax in the formula:
```r
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | classroom) + (1 | classroom:student_id), data = d)
# or equivalently, the shorthand:
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | classroom/student_id), data = d)
```
The classroom/student_id shorthand expands to (1 | classroom) + (1 | classroom:student_id), which constructs a unique identifier for each student by interacting their ID with their classroom.

Option 2 — Create globally unique IDs before fitting:
```r
d$student_uid <- paste(d$classroom, d$student_id, sep = "_")
lmer(y ~ x + (1 | classroom) + (1 | student_uid), data = d)
```

Quick diagnostic to run before fitting:
```r
# TRUE → IDs are globally unique
# FALSE → IDs are reused across classrooms; must use nesting syntax or recode.
n_distinct(d$student_id) == nrow(unique(d[, c("classroom", "student_id")]))
```

Bottom line: (1 | classroom) + (1 | student_id) is wrong here. Use (1 | classroom/student_id) or create globally unique IDs first.
